Word limits as in CBSE: VSA 40 words, SA 60, case-based 100, LA 120.
Map questions appear here as place-identification items (the form CBSE uses for visually impaired candidates). Also practise them on a printed outline map of India.

Written answers: write on paper (or type in the box). After you submit, compare with the model answer and award your own marks point by point, the way a board examiner uses the marking scheme.
Internal choice: tap Option A or Option B and answer only that one.
The timer runs for the full 3 hours as a guide; nothing is cut off. Time spent in each section is shown in your report.

questions.topic: Nationalism in the Balkans and Greece
questions.question: The treaty that recognised Greece as an independent nation in 1832 was the:
questions.explanation: Greece's struggle for independence began in 1821 and ended with the Treaty of Constantinople, 1832.

questions.question: The Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in:
questions.explanation: A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919; Gandhiji saw it as a chance to bring Muslims into a unified national movement.

questions.topic: Print and social reform in India
questions.question: Who wrote 'Gulamgiri' (1871) about the injustices of the caste system?
questions.explanation: Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of 'low caste' protest movements, wrote Gulamgiri in 1871.

questions.question: The 'silk routes' are a good example of:
options: railway networks built under colonial rule
sea routes discovered by European explorers in the 1500s
vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world
routes used only to carry Chinese silk to India
questions.explanation: Silk routes carried goods, people, ideas and religions (Buddhism, Christianity, Islam) between Asia, Europe and northern Africa.

questions.question: Explain any two features of the Civil Code of 1804 (the Napoleonic Code).
questions.model_answer:
It did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.
In the territories under French control it simplified administration, abolished the feudal system, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, and removed guild restrictions in towns. (Any two.)

alts.question: Why did the Non-Cooperation Movement slow down in the cities?
alts.model_answer:
Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, and poor people could not afford it.
The boycott of British institutions needed Indian alternatives, but these came up slowly, so students and teachers drifted back to government schools and lawyers to courts.
(Also: the movement shifted its energy to the countryside.)
alts.label: A

alts.question: How did print help the growth of nationalism in nineteenth-century India?
alts.model_answer:
Newspapers and journals in many Indian languages reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities.
Print carried debates on social and religious reform to a wide public, connecting people across regions.
When the government tried to control the press through the Vernacular Press Act (1878), nationalist newspapers protested, and the repression itself fuelled more criticism and solidarity.
alts.label: B

alts.question: Describe the process of the unification of Italy.
alts.model_answer:
In the mid-nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states; only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house.
Giuseppe Mazzini formed the secret society Young Italy to spread the goal of a unitary Italian republic, but the revolutionary uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed.
Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II then took the lead. Chief minister Cavour, through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France, defeated the Austrian forces in 1859.
In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi led armed volunteers (the Red Shirts) into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and drove out the Spanish rulers.
In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

rubric.p: Cavour's alliance with France; Austria defeated 1859
Victor Emmanuel II king of united Italy, 1861

alts.label: A

alts.question: How did the First World War create a new economic and political situation in India?
alts.model_answer:
Defence expenditure rose sharply; it was financed by war loans and higher taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax introduced.
Prices increased: between 1913 and 1918 they doubled, causing extreme hardship for the common people.
Villages were called upon to supply soldiers, and forced recruitment in rural areas caused widespread anger.
In 1918-19 and 1920-21 crops failed in many parts of India, causing acute food shortages, and an influenza epidemic followed; 12 to 13 million people died from famines and the epidemic.
People hoped hardships would end after the war, but they did not; a new leader, Gandhiji, offered a new mode of struggle.

rubric.p: War expenditure: loans, taxes, customs, income tax
Crop failures and influenza; 12–13 million deaths

alts.label: B

questions.stem:
Read the source.
Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation. In the twentieth century this sense of collective belonging came partly through cultural processes: history and fiction, folklore and songs, popular prints and symbols. The identity of India came to be visually associated with the image of Bharat Mata, and nationalists recorded folk tales and songs in villages. (Our summary, based on NCERT Class 10 History, Chapter 2.)

parts.question: The famous image of Bharat Mata was painted by:
parts.explanation: Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata as an ascetic figure: calm, composed, divine and spiritual.

parts.question: Who wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland?
parts.model_answer: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (in the 1870s; later included in his novel Anandamath).

parts.question: Explain two ways in which folklore and symbols created a sense of nationalism.
parts.model_answer:
Folk tales and songs were seen as giving a true picture of traditional culture damaged by outside forces; preserving them helped people discover a national identity and a pride in the past.
Symbols such as flags united people: the Swadeshi flag (red, green, yellow with eight lotuses) in Bengal, and by 1921 a tricolour with a spinning wheel; carrying the flag in marches was a symbol of defiance.

rubric.p: Symbols such as flags unite and inspire defiance

questions.explanation: Laterite soil forms under intense leaching in hot, wet areas.

questions.explanation: Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada in Gujarat (the Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed it).

questions.explanation: Farmers clear a patch of land, grow crops for the family and move on when fertility falls.

questions.explanation: Anthracite has the most carbon; lignite is low-grade brown coal, peat the lowest.

questions.question: Which of these is a mineral-based industry?
questions.explanation: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals as raw material.

questions.question: Mention two methods of controlling soil erosion in hilly areas.
questions.model_answer:
Contour ploughing (ploughing along contour lines) decelerates the flow of water down the slopes.
Terrace farming (steps cut on slopes) restricts erosion; strip cropping and shelter belts also help. (Any two.)

alts.question: How do industries cause environmental degradation? Suggest measures to control it.
alts.model_answer:
Air pollution: smoke from chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants, burning fossil fuels; it harms health and causes acid rain.
Water pollution: organic and inorganic industrial effluents (paper, pulp, chemical, textile, dyeing, petroleum, tanneries) discharged into rivers.
Thermal pollution: hot water from factories and thermal plants drained into rivers before cooling. Noise pollution: hearing problems and stress.
Measures: minimising use of water by reuse and recycling; rainwater harvesting; treating hot water and effluents before release (primary, secondary, tertiary treatment); fitting electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and filters to smokestacks; using oil or gas instead of coal; machinery redesigned to reduce noise.
alts.label: A

alts.question: Why were multipurpose river projects called the 'temples of modern India'? Why have they faced opposition in recent years?
alts.model_answer:
Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would integrate development of agriculture and the village economy with rapid industrialisation and growth of the urban economy.
They serve many purposes: irrigation, electricity generation, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding.
Opposition: they affect the natural flow of rivers, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the reservoir bed; they fragment rivers, making migration difficult for aquatic fauna; they submerge vegetation and soil; local people are displaced and lose their land and livelihood (e.g. Narmada Bachao Andolan, Tehri Dam Andolan); and they can cause floods, induce earthquakes and water-borne diseases.

rubric.p: Effects on rivers / sediment / aquatic life
Displacement of local people with example

alts.label: B

questions.stem:
Read the source.
Minerals are a finite and non-renewable resource. The geological processes that form them are so slow that their rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with the present rate of consumption. Continued extraction of ores leads to increasing costs as mineral extraction comes from greater depths, along with a decrease in quality. (Our summary, based on NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 5.)

parts.question: Minerals are called non-renewable because:
options: they cannot be used again once mined
they are found only in India
their formation takes millions of years
they are always found deep underground
parts.explanation: Replenishment is extremely slow compared with how fast we use them.

parts.question: Suggest one way to conserve mineral resources.
parts.model_answer: Use improved technologies to use low-grade ores at lower cost, or recycle metals using scrap metals and other substitutes.

parts.question: Why is it necessary to conserve mineral resources? Give two reasons.
parts.model_answer: Minerals are finite and non-renewable; reserves can run out. Continued extraction makes it costlier, as mining goes deeper and ore quality falls.

rubric.p: Rising cost and falling quality of extraction

questions.question: Sharing of power between governments at different levels (union, state, local) is called:
questions.explanation: Horizontal division is among organs (legislature, executive, judiciary) at the same level.

questions.question: Which country is an example of a 'coming together' federation?
questions.explanation: Independent states came together to form a bigger unit (USA, Switzerland, Australia).

questions.question: The 'sexual division of labour' means:
options: women are reserved one-third of seats
the belief that housework and bringing up children are women's work, while men work outside
men and women get equal wages
men and women work in separate factories
questions.explanation: It is a social expectation, not biology.

questions.question: Which country is an example of a one-party system?
questions.explanation: In China only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.

questions.question: Give two prudential reasons for power sharing.
questions.model_answer:
Power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups.
Since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, power sharing ensures the stability of political order.

questions.question: Why is a democratic government called a legitimate government? Give two reasons.
questions.model_answer:
It is the people's own government, chosen through free and fair elections.
It is accountable to citizens, and decisions are taken through proper norms and procedures, so people accept them.

questions.question: State three functions of political parties in a democracy.
questions.model_answer:
Parties contest elections and put forward candidates.
They put forward policies and programmes for voters to choose from.
They make laws through debate in the legislature; they form and run governments, and those that lose play the role of opposition; they shape public opinion and give people access to government machinery and welfare schemes. (Any three.)

alts.question: How does caste influence politics in India? How does politics in turn influence caste?
alts.model_answer:
Caste in politics: parties keep in mind the caste composition of the electorate when choosing candidates; they appeal to caste sentiment to win support; some parties are known to favour some castes; universal adult franchise and one-person-one-vote made leaders mobilise votes.
But caste alone does not decide elections: no constituency has a clear majority of one caste, no party wins all votes of a caste, and voters judge governments on performance.
Politics in caste: each caste tries to become bigger by including neighbouring sub-castes; caste groups ally with others; new kinds of caste groups such as 'backward' and 'forward' have emerged; politics has helped Dalits and OBCs gain better access to decision-making.

rubric.p: Candidates chosen with caste in mind
Caste alone does not decide outcomes
Castes enlarge and ally (politics in caste)
New caste groupings / access for Dalits and OBCs

alts.label: A

alts.question: Explain how federalism has been practised in India through linguistic states, language policy and centre-state relations.
alts.model_answer:
Linguistic states: after 1947 many old states were redrawn so that people speaking the same language lived in the same state; some were created on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography. This made the country more united and administration easier.
Language policy: the Constitution did not give any one language the status of national language; Hindi was identified as the official language, with English also used, and many other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages. States have their own official languages. Leaders adopted a cautious attitude when spreading Hindi.
Centre-state relations: for a long time the same party ruled at the centre and in most states, and the centre sometimes misused the Constitution to dismiss state governments. After 1990 the era of coalition governments at the centre led to a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of state governments; a Supreme Court judgment made it difficult to dismiss state governments arbitrarily.
alts.label: B

questions.stem:
Read the source.
Is democracy good for economic growth? Considering all democracies and all dictatorships over fifty years between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships have a slightly higher rate of growth. But this cannot be the only reason to reject democracy: growth also depends on population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries and the economic priorities adopted. Within democracies, economic inequality remains high. (Our summary, based on NCERT Class 10 Political Science, Chapter 5.)

parts.question: Which outcome is a democracy expected to produce above all?
options: The highest rate of economic growth in the world
A government that is accountable and responsive to citizens
parts.explanation: Accountable, responsive and legitimate government is democracy's basic outcome.

parts.question: Why does economic inequality pose a challenge to democracy?
parts.model_answer: The poor form a large share of voters, yet their needs often go unmet; this can reduce their faith in democratic governments.

rubric.p: Poor voters' needs unmet → loss of faith

parts.question: Give two ways in which democracy promotes the dignity and freedom of individuals.
parts.model_answer:
It has strengthened the claims of women for respect and equal treatment.
It has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and opportunity.

questions.question: A likely development goal of a landless rural labourer is:
options: more days of work and better wages
questions.explanation: Different people have different developmental goals depending on their situation.

questions.question: The Human Development Report, which compares countries on health, education and income, is published by the:
questions.explanation: The United Nations Development Programme publishes the HDR.

questions.question: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of:
options: all goods, including intermediate goods, produced in a year
all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
questions.explanation: Only final goods are counted to avoid double counting.

questions.question: Which of these is a formal source of credit?
questions.explanation: Banks and cooperatives are formal sources supervised by the RBI.

questions.question: A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation is called a:
questions.explanation: MNCs set up offices and factories where they get cheap labour, resources and markets.

questions.topic: Money as a medium of exchange
questions.question: 'Double coincidence of wants' means:
options: what one person wants to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy, and the other way round
both people use the same currency
two banks lend to the same person
prices of two goods rise together
questions.explanation: Barter needs this coincidence; money removes the need for it.

questions.question: Suggest three ways in which more employment can be created in rural areas.
questions.model_answer:
Government investment in irrigation (wells, check dams) lets farmers grow a second crop, employing more people.
Better roads, transport and storage (cold storage, godowns) create jobs and help farmers sell in markets.
Cheap credit from banks for farming; promoting agro-processing industries and small-scale units (e.g. a dal mill, honey collection, cold storage); jobs in tourism, education and health. (Any three.)

questions.question: How does the Reserve Bank of India supervise the functioning of formal sources of loans?
questions.model_answer:
The RBI checks that banks actually maintain the cash balance it prescribes (a minimum share of deposits).
It sees that banks give loans not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers.
Banks must submit information periodically to the RBI on how much they lend, to whom and at what interest rate.

rubric.p: Loans to small borrowers, not only big business

questions.question: What is meant by liberalisation of trade? Why did the Indian government remove barriers to foreign trade and investment around 1991?
questions.model_answer:
Liberalisation means removing barriers or restrictions set by the government, e.g. on imports and foreign investment.
After independence, India had restricted foreign trade and investment to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.
Around 1991 the government decided Indian producers were ready to compete; competition would improve their quality, so barriers were removed to a large extent.

alts.question: Explain the impact of globalisation on India. Is it shared equally by all?
alts.model_answer:
Consumers, especially the well-off in urban areas, have greater choice, better quality and lower prices.
MNCs have increased investment in India, creating new jobs; local companies supplying them have prospered.
Some large Indian companies have become multinationals themselves (e.g. Tata Motors, Infosys).
New opportunities have opened up in services, especially IT.
Not shared equally: small producers (e.g. in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy, edible oil) were hit hard by competition and many units shut down; workers face uncertain, flexible jobs with long hours and fewer benefits. Fair globalisation needs government policies that protect workers and small producers.

rubric.p: Workers' insecurity / need for fair globalisation

alts.label: A

alts.question: What are 'terms of credit'? Explain them with an example, and say why formal credit should be expanded.
alts.model_answer:
Terms of credit are the conditions of a loan: the interest rate, collateral, documentation required and the mode of repayment.
Example: a farmer borrows from a bank at a fixed interest rate, pledging land papers as collateral, submitting documents and repaying in instalments after harvest; terms vary by lender and borrower.
Informal lenders charge much higher interest, so more of the borrower's income goes in repayment and debt can trap them.
Formal credit is cheaper and safer, so banks and cooperatives should lend more, especially in rural areas, and credit should be shared more equally so the poor can benefit.
alts.label: B
